lesson.menu_title: The Numbers Room — Results for People Who Do Not Read Numbers
lesson.menu_desc: Explaining a year of results to a chief executive who is not from finance, and saying who did what without saying I -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- The Numbers Room
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 16 -- The Numbers Room
phases: The Words of a Results Talk

listenings.text: I came up through the creative side, and for years I sat through results presentations I did not understand. What changed it was one finance director who started every meeting with a single sentence. Revenue is up eight percent year on year, the margin is down one point, and here is why. Then he told me which part was a one-off and which part would still be there next quarter. That is all I need from a CFO. I do not need every line. I need to know what happened, whether it will happen again, and what is being done about it. When a candidate for that job cannot give me those three things in plain English, I assume he cannot give them to my board either.

On a board you hear the same phrases every quarter. It is expected that the market will recover in the second half. The decline is believed to be temporary. Those sentences are not wrong, but I have learned to ask who expects it and who believes it. The finance directors I trust answer that straight away. We had the forecast reviewed by the two largest clients, and both of them confirmed the volume. That is a different sentence. It tells me the work was done and who did it. When a candidate uses the passive to hide where a number came from, I notice. When he uses it to show that somebody checked, I notice that too.

extra_audio.text: Marta asks him to explain the year as he would to her board. He opens with one sentence: revenue up, margin down, and why. He separates the one-off cost from the part that will stay. He says the forecast was reviewed by the two largest clients. He finishes with what is being done, and hands the question back.

reading.rtitle: Why boards stop listening to the finance director
paras: It is often said that boards do not understand numbers. Most of the non-executive directors interviewed for this note disagreed. They understand numbers well enough; what they do not understand is a presentation that starts with forty lines of a spreadsheet and never says which three of them matter.

The finance directors who are listened to work the other way round. They open with one sentence that a person from sales or from the creative side could repeat in the corridor: revenue is up, the margin is down, and this is why. Only then do they separate what happened once from what will still be there next quarter. A one-off cost explained in the first minute is a detail. The same cost discovered in the appendix is a credibility problem.

The third habit is about where the numbers came from. A forecast that is simply described as expected tells a board very little. A forecast that was reviewed by the two largest clients, or that the CFO had checked by an outside firm, tells the board that somebody did the work. Directors said they trusted the passive when it named the check, and distrusted it when it hid the person behind the number.
None of this requires simpler numbers. It requires a finance director who has decided, before the meeting, which sentence the board should leave with, and who can say it in plain English.
reading.source: Adapted from board practice notes on finance reporting

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Boards need simpler numbers because most directors cannot read a spreadsheet or an appendix.
Directors listen to the CFO who leads with one clear sentence and says where the numbers came from.
Finance directors should leave one-off costs in the appendix.
